title: How do I run simulations and a power analysis to test for a 2 x 2 x 2 interaction?
body:
I conducted two 2 x 2 SPR studies in Spanish based on [Kush, Lidz, & Phillips (2015)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0749596X15000224?casa_token=etTE-PhjaL8AAAAA:sRaGSWa5n9bhm5p32J7Ibq9Ar3GbLTwB6prVwW1ttepofFBH8bpic-5Rqbm4t7MFjxYN3dTKLw). 

Both experiments manipulated the factors NP Referentiality (NP | QP) and GenderMatch between the NP/QP in an RC and a later pronoun in the MC (Match | Mismatch). We ran these studies in Spanish because it allows both preverbal and postverbal object pronouns. Accordingly, critical pronouns were preverbal in Exp. 1 and postverbal in Exp. 2. 

The question I want to answer is whether pronoun position (preverbal vs. postverbal) modulates interference from gender-matching but structurally-inappropriate QPs. To do so, I need to run a 2 x 2 x 2 experiment with the factors NP Referentiality, GenderMatch and Position and test for a 3-way interaction. 

**Goal:** Figure out how to run simulations and a power analysis to find out how many participants I'd need to find the 3-way interaction, if it were there.

**My repo:** [https://github.com/jorquer4/BV-Project](url)
**The .csv file containing the combined data for both experiments:** [https://github.com/jorquer4/BV-Project/blob/main/merged_bv_data.csv](url)
**The .csv file with just the preverbal experiment:** [https://github.com/jorquer4/BV-Project/blob/main/PrevExpData.csv](url)
**The .csv file with just the postverbal experiment:**
My R code with some descriptives, graphs and a lmer model: [https://github.com/jorquer4/BV-Project/blob/main/BV_Power_Analysis.R](url)
**My MA thesis, which talks about each experiment in length:** [https://github.com/jorquer4/BV-Project/blob/main/jorquera_forum_paper.pdf](url)

**Question:** Should I go Bayesian with either my models, the power analysis or both?

Thanks so much!

comments.body:
Hi,
 
```
NOTE TO FUTURE READERS: Even though the overall idea is good here, 
it is very inefficient. See the next comment and also this code 
for the efficient version: 
https://github.com/utkuturk/bcms-prefix-production/blob/main/power_analysis.r
```

I think the loop suggested in Vasishth et al. 2020 is what you might need: https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s42113-021-00125-y.pdf 

As for choice of 'bayesian' vs. 'glmer', I do not see any reason not to go bayesian and use brms. The only worry is that since this is going to be 100s of simulations, it can take a lot of time. Luckily, you can use the umd cluster.

Of course 1 questions still is there. 
- Sampling priors 

I would first analyze the KLP2015 paper and get the numbers. I would use those numbers as the fixed manipulate the relevant range for the interaction. 


```r
fe <- fixef(m.klp2015)

imean <- fe["Intercept", "Estimate"]
ierror <- fe["Intercept", "Est.Error"]
f1mean <- fe["factor1", "Estimate"]
f1error <- fe["factor1", "Est.Error"]
```


And then I would set the base priors. 


```r
basepriors <- c(
  ## these are klpmodel
  set_prior(sprintf("normal(%.4f, %.4f)", imean,  ierror), class = "Intercept"),
  set_prior(sprintf("normal(%.4f, %.4f)", f1mean,  f1error), class = "b", coef = "factor1"),
  set_prior(sprintf("normal(%.4f, %.4f)", f2mean,  f2error), class = "b", coef = "factor2"),
  set_prior(sprintf("normal(%.4f, %.4f)", int12mean, int12error), class = "b", coef = "factor1:factor2"),
  set_prior("exponential(1)", class = "sd")
)
```

now using these base priors from their model, you can operationalize the interaction priors. I have no clue about your factor3, so I will just assume random stuff. 

```r
make_custom_priors <- function(basepriors, int3mean, int3error, f3mean=NULL, f3error=NULL,) {
  
  # you can hardcode these or pass them as arguments
  new_priors <- c(
    set_prior(sprintf("normal(%.4f, %.4f)", f3mean, f3error), class = "b", coef = "factor3"),
    # Keeping the 2-way interactions with factor 3 stable (e.g., Mean 0, SD 1)
    set_prior("normal(0, 1)", class = "b", coef = "factor1:factor3"),
    set_prior("normal(0, 1)", class = "b", coef = "factor2:factor3"),
    
    # 4. The "Important One" - The 3-way interaction
    set_prior(sprintf("normal(%.4f, %.4f)", int3mean, int3error), class = "b", coef = "factor1:factor2:factor3")
  )
  
  return(basepriors + new_priors)
}

sampling_priors <- make_custom_priors(
  basepriors = basepriors, 
  f3error = 0.5, f3error = 0.1, # Factor 3 small but significant effect
  int3mean = 1, int3error = 0.2  # Really clear 3-way interaction. 
)

```

I would say a better approach would be to create more conservative than normal(1,0.2), or maybe a range of priors. 

but now we need a model to loop through and extract values. 

Here's a faster version with p values. I dont know why anyone would use this if they have power to do 1000 simulations. 

```r

create_experiment_data <- function(n_subs, n_items) {
  expand.grid(
    participant = paste0("p_", 1:n_subs),
    item        = paste0("i_", 1:n_items),
    factor1     = c("A", "B"),
    factor2     = c("C", "D"),
    factor3     = c("E", "F")
  )
}

get_p_simulated <- function(mypriors, n_subs = 30, n_items = 40) {
  
  # dummy data for the brms function
  dummy_data <- create_experiment_data(2, 2) 
  dummy_data$answer_binary <- 0
  
  prior_model <- brm(
    answer_binary ~ factor1 * factor2 * factor3 + (1|participant) + (1|item), # something like this, include random effects too etc. 
    data = dummy_data, 
    family = bernoulli(),
    prior = mypriors,
    sample_prior = "only",
    chains = 4, iter = 4000,  # change this to your liking
    silent = 2, refresh = 0,
    backend = "cmdstanr"
  )
  
  # new data for the predictions
  new_experiment <- create_experiment_data(n_subs, n_items)

  yrep <- posterior_predict(
    prior_model,
    newdata = new_experiment,
    allow_new_levels = TRUE,
    sample_new_levels = "gaussian"
  )
  
  new_experiment$answer_binary <- yrep[1, ]

  # do simple glm 
  # I would instead of this use another brms model 
  # and also would include random effects
  fit <- glm(
    answer_binary ~ factor1 * factor2 * factor3,
    data = new_experiment, 
    family = binomial
  )
  
  # extract p 
  coef_names <- rownames(summary(fit)$coefficients)
  target_coef <- coef_names[grep("factor1.*factor2.*factor3", coef_names)]
  
  p <- summary(fit)$coefficients[target_coef, "Pr(>|z|)"]
  
  p
}

```


now we find a way to analyse the power, which is basically means of how many times p exceed 0.05

```r

calculate_power <- function(target_priors, n_subs = 100, n_items = 40, n_sim = 1000) {
  
  results <- replicate(n_sim, get_p_simulated(target_priors, n_subs = n_subs, n_items = n_items))
  
  power_val <- mean(results < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
  
  list(
    power = power_val,
    p_values = results,
    n_subs = n_subs
  )
}

```


now you do it for a range of participants and then print the table or curve whatever you want


```r

# Testing 20, 40, 60, 80, 100 participants
sub_range <- seq(20, 100, by = 20) 
power_by_n <- lapply(sub_range, function(n) {
  res <- calculate_power(
    target_priors = fixed_effect_prior, 
    n_subs = n, 
    n_items = 40, 
    n_sim = 1000 # reduce the number if you want to lose stability but gain fastness
  )
  
  data.frame(n_participants = n, power = res$power)
})

power_table <- do.call(rbind, power_by_n)
print(power_table)
```

and then you can plot it too

```r

get_curve <- function(table) {

ggplot(table, aes(x = n_participants, y = power)) +
  geom_line(size = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.80, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  theme_minimal()

}

get_curve(power_table)
```



I would rather you do brms in both parts of get_p. requires more decisions. in the second half of the model do this instead

```r
fit <- brm(
    answer_binary ~ factor1 * factor2 * factor3 + (1|participant) + (1|item),
    data = new_experiment, family = bernoulli(),
    # Use generic weakly informative priors for the test so we don't "cheat"
    prior = set_prior("normal(0, 5)", class = "b"), 
    chains = 2, iter = 1000, warmup = 500, # Lower iters for speed
    silent = 2, refresh = 0, backend = "cmdstanr"
  )

  # check if the 95% credible interval excludes zero
  post_summary <- fixef(fit)
  target_row <- rownames(post_summary)[grep("factor1:factor2:factor3", rownames(post_summary))]
  
  lower_bound <- post_summary[target_row, "Q2.5"]
  upper_bound <- post_summary[target_row, "Q97.5"]
  
  is_significant <- ifelse(lower_bound > 0 | upper_bound < 0, 1, 0)
  
  return(is_significant)

```

significance with bayesian is a funny term. basically it is a made up concept and you say whether if it crosses 0. Vasishth and Nicenboim repeatedly says not to do this. I ll later tell you another possibility. for now let's do the funny thing. the rest from here is the same 


```r
# assuming you ran bunch of stuff already and just updated the get_p... function

power_table <- do.call(rbind, power_by_n)
print(power_table)
get_curve(power_table)

```



Again if you have enough power you can just  store all the estimated values. not just the p or mean or something. the last part of the get_p can be updated like this, so no fixef(fit) or whatever. 

```r

post_samples <- fit %>%
    spread_draws(b_factor1:factor2:factor3) %>%
    rename(interaction_effect = `b_factor1:factor2:factor3`) %>%
    select(interaction_effect)
  
  return(post_samples$interaction_effect)
```

since these are a more than a single value for a simulation, you will have repeated values 


```r
n_sim <- 1000
all_sims_data <- data.frame()

for(range_value in sub_range) {
  for(i in 1:n_sim) {
    # vector of posteriors 
    draws <- get_p_simulated(target_priors, n_subs = range_value, n_items = 40)
    
    # bind them
    temp_df <- data.frame(
      n_subs = n,
      sim_id = i,
      draw = draws
    )
    all_sims_data <- rbind(all_sims_data, temp_df)
  }
}
```


And then you can plot the **UNCERTAINTY OF UNCERTAINTY**, i actually like this lol

```r

ggplot(all_sims_data, aes(x = draw, group = interaction(n_subs, sim_id), color = as.factor(n_subs))) +
  geom_density(size = 0.8, alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dotted", size = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~n_subs) +
  labs(
    title = "simulated posteriors",
    subtitle = "each curve is a separate simulated experiment",
    x = "Interaction effect size",
    y = "Density",
    color = "N Participants"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```


from this you can go back to the p thing again if you want


```r
power_summary <- all_sims_data %>%
  group_by(n_subs, sim_id) %>%
  summarize(
    # Does 95% of the posterior sit on one side of zero?
    is_significant = (quantile(draw, 0.025) > 0 | quantile(draw, 0.975) < 0)
  ) %>%
  group_by(n_subs) %>%
  summarize(power = mean(is_significant))

print(power_summary)
```

hope this helps

comments.body:
Here's an example code that I code it for myself. After trying myself out, I realized that the model is unneccesarily inefficient: 'brms' model initiation is way too slow. This is because of the fact that brms transform your code into stan code and then runs it. it is way faster to just run the stan code itself. luckily, brms helps you with creating the code, with make_stancode().

secondly, if one needs to go full bayesian (bayesian prior sampling + bayesian posteriors for the simulated data) update() probably is a better approach than just fitting a new model. 

The code I link here is bayesian prior sampling + lmer p values. For 4 participant groups, 1000 simulations, 32 cores, 64 GB CPU, it took 4 days. With stan code, I assume that it would take less than a day. 

But more importantly, one does not need to fit brm() or stan code every time in the simulation. update() function with different seeds is enough. The code I show here, now compile's once and then uses update() following Solomon Kurz: https://solomonkurz.netlify.app/blog/bayesian-power-analysis-part-i/ update() does not compile the stan code again and again.  (I also put my inefficient code commented out) 

[https://github.com/utkuturk/bcms-prefix-production/blob/main/power_analysis.r](https://github.com/utkuturk/bcms-prefix-production/blob/main/power_analysis.r)
